query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Plasma nitriding treatment of titanium alloys (e.g., Ti-6Al-4V) increases the surface hardness and wear resistance by forming a hard, nitrogen-rich surface nitride layer.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard structural titanium alloy such as Ti-6Al-4V in its conventionally processed (annealed or solution-treated and aged) state with a homogenous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Expose the titanium alloy to plasma nitriding by subjecting the surface to a nitrogen plasma under controlled thermal conditions.
generation.conditions: Treatment at approximately 600°C under a low-pressure nitrogen atmosphere for durations on the order of several hours (e.g., 4–6 hours). The improvement is expected to hold under typical service conditions for structural alloys (ambient to moderate elevated temperatures during wear or friction tests such as pin-on-disk under moderate loads).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a surface layer composed primarily of titanium nitrides (e.g., TiN) resulting from the diffusion of nitrogen atoms into the substrate.
generation.mechanism: The nitrogen diffuses into the titanium alloy during the plasma treatment, reacting with titanium to form hard, stable nitride phases at the surface. These nitrides act as a barrier to wear and abrasion, thereby increasing the surface hardness and improving wear resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in surface hardness as measured by microhardness or nanoindentation tests (with expected increases possibly in the range of 20-50% over untreated material, though the exact percentage is uncertain) and improved wear resistance in standardized wear tests.
generation.baseline: Untreated or conventionally processed titanium alloy having lower surface hardness and higher wear rate under similar test conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies when the plasma nitriding conditions maintain a controlled temperature and exposure to avoid unwanted grain growth or excessive internal stresses that could detrimentally affect the core properties of the alloy.
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvement magnitude is uncertain due to potential variability in process parameters and titanium alloy microstructure. Also, the uniformity and adhesion of the nitride layer may vary with processing details.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti-6Al-4V samples: one set undergoing plasma nitriding under the specified conditions, and one untreated control group. Conduct standardized surface hardness measurements (e.g., nanoindentation or Vickers microhardness tests) and wear resistance tests (e.g., pin-on-disk under controlled loads and speeds).
measurements: Surface hardness values across a depth profile of the treated layer
Mass loss or wear track depth/volume during wear tests
Examination of the microstructural phase composition of the surface layer via X-ray diffraction (XRD) or scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the plasma nitrided samples do not show a statistically significant increase in surface hardness and a corresponding reduction in wear (e.g., less than a 10-15% improvement over the control samples) under the specified test conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
